section.title: General power rule and hyperbolic functions

introduction.p: For x>0, logarithms extend the power rule to every real exponent: (x^r)\prime=rx^{r-1}. This section proves that result, defines hyperbolic functions using exponentials, and develops their identities, inverses, and derivatives.

exercise.title: Why does the power formula not automatically settle x=0?

statement.p: The cube root is defined at 0, but its difference quotient becomes unbounded there. In your own words, why must the point x=0 be checked separately, even after the general power rule is known?

hint.p: A formula on x>0 does not decide a two-sided derivative at the origin. The function may exist at 0 while no finite tangent slope exists.

subsection.title: Inverse hyperbolic functions: branches and derivatives
subsection.p: The identity \cosh^2 t-\sinh^2 t=1 gives the derivatives of the inverses once we choose their branches. We use the names \operatorname{arsinh}, \operatorname{arcosh}, and \operatorname{artanh} to avoid confusing an inverse with a reciprocal. For example, \operatorname{arsinh}x is an inverse function, whereas \operatorname{csch}x=1/\sinh x.
Complete the family by defining \coth t=\cosh t/\sinh t and \operatorname{csch}t=1/\sinh t for t\ne0. The quotient and reciprocal rules give

Since \cosh t>0, \sinh is strictly increasing from \mathbb R onto \mathbb R. The function \tanh is strictly increasing from \mathbb R onto (-1,1). The even functions \cosh and \operatorname{sech} must be restricted to t\ge0 to have inverses. For \coth and \operatorname{csch}, the positive and negative branches have disjoint ranges, so both branches can be inverted together.
Solving the exponential definitions gives logarithmic formulas on precisely these domains:

For example, write x=\sinh y and set z=e^y>0. Then z^2-2xz-1=0, whose positive root is x+\sqrt{x^2+1}. Taking its logarithm proves the first formula. For x=\cosh y, the roots are x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}; the branch y\ge0 selects the plus sign. Solving x=(e^{2y}-1)/(e^{2y}+1) proves the formula for \operatorname{artanh}. The other formulas follow by taking reciprocals in these three inverse relations.

figure.caption: The three basic inverse branches. The branch of \operatorname{arcosh} begins at (1,0); \operatorname{artanh} has vertical asymptotes at x=\pm1.

description.p: Separate plots of arsinh on the real line, arcosh for x at least one, and artanh between minus one and one, with dashed vertical asymptotes for artanh.

subsection.p: For y=\operatorname{arsinh}x, implicit differentiation gives 1=\cosh y\,y'. Since \cosh y=\sqrt{1+x^2}>0, the first derivative follows. For y=\operatorname{arcosh}x with x>1, we have y>0 and \sinh y=\sqrt{x^2-1}. For \operatorname{artanh} and \operatorname{arcoth}, the logarithmic formulas immediately give 1/(1-x^2). Finally, \operatorname{arsech}x=\operatorname{arcosh}(1/x) and \operatorname{arcsch}x=\operatorname{arsinh}(1/x); the chain rule gives the last two formulas. In the last calculation, \sqrt{1+1/x^2}=\sqrt{1+x^2}/|x|, so the absolute value cannot be dropped.

warning.title: The endpoints still matter
warning.p: The functions \operatorname{arcosh} and \operatorname{arsech} are defined at x=1, but they have no finite one-sided derivative there. Also, \operatorname{arcosh}(\cosh t)=|t|, whereas \operatorname{arsinh}(\sinh t)=t. The restriction used to define an inverse remains part of the answer.

subsection.p: This is a good preview of differential equations. A physical law can describe a curve by a relation among its derivatives. Solving the law means finding a function with exactly that derivative behavior.
Hyperbolic functions are useful because they are built from exponentials and have simple derivative cycles:
They are not just extra names. They package the functions that naturally solve some laws of growth, balance, and shape.

subsection.title: The derivative table at the end of Chapter 5
subsection.p: Chapter 5 has built a large but organized table of derivatives:

p.me: \begin{array}{c|c} \text{function} \amp \text{derivative}\\ \hline x^r \amp rx^{r-1}\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ \arcsin x \amp \dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arctan x \amp \dfrac1{1+x^2}\\ \sinh x \amp \cosh x\\ \cosh x \amp \sinh x \end{array}

subsection.p: The rules behind the table are just as important as the table itself:

p.me: \text{sum rule, product rule, quotient rule, chain rule, inverse rule.}

subsection.p: These rules let us differentiate complicated functions by reading how they are built.
